messages.subject: GGIR for non-human (animal) research?
parts:
Hello,

I'm looking to see if anyone has used any of the GGIR compatible devices on non-human research? I used the Activinsights GENEActiv accelerometers to track activity patterns in lemurs and was wondering if I can still use the GGIR package for analysis. I know that I will need to change some of the default arguments but wanted to check what others have done. 

Thanks,
Abby

messages.author: 017566be30afa7f3
messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] GGIR for non-human (animal) research?
parts:
Hello Abby,

Cuong Ngo contacted me a while ago about using GGIR algorithms in Whales. I am not sure whether he was using GGIR or had his own software implementation.

Either way, I think you could use GGIR part 1 and 2 for any organism or even non-living objects to describe their acceleration and estimate their orientation.Maybe start with the functionality related to arguments ilevels, qlevels, and qwindow.

The sleep detection in GGIR part 3 and 4 should also work well if you figure out an optimal setting for the angle and time threshold of the algorithm. However, the underlyig assumption is that the species sleep/wakes with 24 hour rhythm and that the main sleep period happens at night. It may not work well if used in species that sleep/wake with alternative rhythms or who are awake at night and have their main sleep period in the middle of the day.

Note that the auto-calibration function in GGIR part 1 works best if the sensor is kept still from time to time in wide range of orientations relative to the horizontal plane. For human behaviour this is no problem, but if you are studying an animal that never rotates relative to the horizontal plane then that could be tricky. In that case I would recommend not using the acceleration metrics that rely on knowledge about gravity (ENMO, EN, ENMOa, LFENMO, HFENplus). Instead, you may want to use BFEN which also is a good indicator of the magnitude of acceleration and is easy to explain as it has been used for decades across scientific fields. Although not under the name BFEN but the concept of band-pass filtering is well established.

Finally, I know that Cassim Ladha has been specialising in animal tracking and is CEO of a company that offers services on this: https://vetsens.co.uk/. I am almost certain he does not use GGIR, but you may want to reach out to him for feedback.

Thanks,
Vincent

Dr. Vincent van Hees | Independent consultant | https://accelting.com/

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] GGIR for non-human (animal) research?
parts:
... correction, I need to phrase one part more specifically:

GGIR is able to handle daysleepers/night workers, but if you are studying animal species  that are awake at night it may depend on how their sleeping patterns. GGIR makes the assumption that sleep occurs between noon and the next noon or between 6 pm and the next 6pm (shiftworkers). So, if your specifies frequently violates both scenarios and for example has sleep stints that start before noon and end after 6pm then GGIR may struggle to make sense of it.
